title: Gradient, Hessian and stationary points
description: Differentiate a two-parameter function, compute curvature directions, and classify minima, maxima and saddles with full practice answers.
source: Lecture3 PDF pages115-121: derivatives/Hessian, pages122-132: stationary points; Lecture4 PDF pages37-49: multivariate quadratics; numerical-practice.md N4.3. Original numerical examples.

pages.title: A slope tells us which way changes the loss
pages.subtitle: Use two parameters x and y, collected into the vector w = (x,y).
blocks: A partial derivative measures change when one parameter moves and the other stays fixed. The gradient collects these slopes into a vector.
Curvature means how a slope itself changes as we move. The Hessian collects derivatives of gradient components. Our tuples list those components; the notes write the gradient as a column vector.
This original study example is N4.3. It has the quadratic form on Lecture4 PDF page37 with A equal to its Hessian, and b = 0, c = 0.

pages.title: Differentiate one parameter at a time
pages.subtitle: Treat the other parameter as a constant.
blocks: For the xy term, y behaves like a fixed coefficient when x changes. The y-squared term is constant with respect to x.
At (2,0), increasing x a little increases E about 6 times that increment; increasing y a little increases E about 2 times that increment.

pages.title: Check what those slopes mean numerically
pages.subtitle: Small changes connect a derivative to something you can calculate.
blocks: The slight difference is the quadratic curvature contribution. A derivative is a local rate, not an exact finite-change formula.

pages.title: Differentiate the slopes to form the Hessian
pages.subtitle: Rows name the gradient component; columns name the parameter being changed.
blocks: Thus H has rows (3,1) and (1,3). The off-diagonal 1 values come from the mixed term xy: moving y changes the x-slope, and moving x changes the y-slope.
These slope changes are exact here because the gradient is linear. The Hessian is constant for this quadratic.

pages.title: Find a stationary point before classifying it
pages.subtitle: Stationary means every first derivative is zero.
blocks: A zero gradient says the first-order slope vanishes. It does not tell us whether the point is a minimum, maximum or saddle.
To distinguish them, inspect how the function curves in different directions near that point.

pages.title: Eigenvalues describe directional curvature
pages.subtitle: An eigenvector is a nonzero direction v for which H v = lambda v.
blocks: The matrix changes the length or sign of this direction, without rotating it to another line. Lambda is the corresponding scale factor. For a unit direction, it is the quadratic curvature.
I is the identity matrix: diagonal entries 1 and off-diagonal entries 0. H - lambda I therefore has rows (3-lambda,1) and (1,3-lambda).
For a 2-by-2 matrix with rows (a,b) and (c,d), its determinant is ad-bc. Set this determinant to zero to find the possible eigenvalues.

pages.title: Verify both eigenvector directions by multiplication
pages.subtitle: These two independent directions account for the whole two-parameter space.
blocks: Both eigenvalues are positive. This is called positive definite: every nonzero direction has positive quadratic curvature. At our stationary point, that establishes a strict local minimum. Local compares nearby points; strict means every different nearby point is higher. Global compares the entire domain.

pages.title: Derive the two directional curves
pages.subtitle: Substitute the coordinates of each unit direction into the original function.
blocks: The sign of xy changes between the directions; the two square terms stay the same. This is why the same surface has different curvature along different directions.

pages.title: Normalize directions before comparing curvature
pages.subtitle: A unit direction has length 1, so the movement coordinate measures distance.
blocks: The second derivatives with respect to distance t are 2 and 4, exactly the eigenvalues. Using unnormalized (1,1) would give E=4t-squared and second derivative 8 because each unit of t moves farther.

pages.title: Maxima curve down; saddles mix directions
pages.subtitle: Evaluate nearby points to see the distinction directly.
blocks: Its Hessian is -H with eigenvalues -2 and -4. Both are negative, so (0,0) is a strict maximum of M.
At (0,0), the gradient is zero and the Hessian is diagonal (1,-1). One curvature is positive, the other negative: the Hessian is indefinite.
Nearby values occur above and below zero, so the origin is a saddle, not a minimum or maximum.

pages.title: A zero Hessian can leave the test inconclusive
pages.subtitle: Use the original function when second-order information is insufficient.
blocks: The Hessian has diagonal entries 12x-squared and 12y-squared, with zero off-diagonal entries. At (0,0), every Hessian entry is zero.
The second-order test is inconclusive. It does not say there is no minimum.
Fourth powers are nonnegative and both vanish only at the origin. This direct argument proves a strict global minimum.

pages.title: Your turn: classify two fresh functions
pages.subtitle: Find gradients, Hessians, stationary points and curvature signs.
blocks: For Q, also calculate the gradient at (1,-1), solve the two-by-two eigenvalue equation, and verify one eigenvector direction.
For R, explain why the stationary point is a maximum even though its gradient is zero, just like the minimum of Q.
State whether zero Hessian eigenvalues always mean a flat function. Use T from the preceding page to support your answer.

pages.title: Practice Q: derivatives and stationary point
pages.subtitle: Differentiate each term while holding the other variable fixed.
blocks: Differentiate these slopes: H has rows (4,1) and (1,4). The mixed term contributes 1 to each off-diagonal entry.

pages.title: Practice Q: eigenvalues and classification
pages.subtitle: Use the determinant and then check an actual direction.
blocks: Both eigenvalues are positive. The Hessian is positive definite, so the stationary origin is a strict local minimum.
The last expression also proves it is the global minimum: all terms are nonnegative and vanish together only at the origin.

pages.title: Practice R: downward curvature and common errors
pages.subtitle: Stationarity and classification are separate questions.
blocks: Its Hessian is diagonal (-2,-4), so its eigenvalues are -2 and -4. Both are negative: the origin is a strict maximum.
Zero eigenvalues do not imply the function is constant or that no minimum exists. T=x-to-the-fourth+y-to-the-fourth has zero curvature exactly at its minimum but grows away from it.
Common errors: treating the other variable as zero instead of constant, omitting mixed derivatives, calling every zero-gradient point a minimum, or using an unnormalized direction as distance.
